                                                                                  CITY OF CANTERBURY BANKSTOWN ANNUAL REPORT 2023/24

Message from the Mayorand CEO


This 2023/24 Annual Report, including the State of Our City, is presented on behalf of the City of Canterbury
Bankstown. We are lucky to live in such a thriving City, and these reports show the many areas where we excel, our
priorities for the future, and the great outcomes that we are achieving as “together we create a City we love”.

In 2023/24 we were working hard to ensure our lifestyle keeps getting better with over $29 million invested in our
parks, playgrounds, pools, libraries and community halls including:
•                                                                                      Commencing construction on the new Canterbury Leisure and Aquatic Centre;
•                                                                                      New amenities building Ewen Park, Hurlstone Park; and Padstow Park;
•                                                                                              A new destin ation  play  space  at Paul Keatin g Park, Bankstown;
•                                                                                              New sports ligh ting at Picken O val, Ashbury; completion  of  the  Ke lso North  pre cin ct upgrade s, Panania; and
       spor tsfie ld upgrade s at Beaman Park  eastern  fields, Ear lwood; an d
•                                                                                      Concept plannin g for the Campsie Hub - a centr al sp ace f or the  Campsie  C ivic pre cin ct th at will offer a  new cen tral
       librar y, f lexible  community spaces, civic spaces, a music hub, improvemen ts to the Or ion  Cen tre and public domain
       improvements.

Our focus on delivering the basics that are important to you has been unwavering. This includes delivering better
roads infrastructure so residents can get home sooner and safer. Over $19 million was invested in 2023/24 to
upgrade the local transport netwo  rk including:
•                                                                                              Comple tion  of  the Can terbury Road an d Ch arle s S treet in tersection  upgrade ;

       Earlwood; Shellcote Road, Greenacre; Polo Street, Revesby; Penshurst Road, Narwee; and
•                                                                                              An upgrade of the Cup and Saucer Creek shared path.

The safety and amenity of local centres are enlivened with free, affordable events, and distinctive public art and
infrastructure. The Canterbury-                            Bankstown Her-Way project in Lakemba for example, provided temporary
activations co-designed with local women,                 new seating, upgraded lighting and a temporary bike track. Council
also provided over $500,000 for local projects in our annual Community Grants Program, ensuring that local
organisations can deliver meaningful outcomes at the grass roots level.

Partnering with the community, we held many major events to boost our economy, and to attract business
investment, jobs, visitors, and new residents to the City.  The Rocking After Dark –                Night Time Economy event,
"Where Interesting Happens” website and initiatives, Youth Expo, CBEvolve event, Bankstown +10 event, and
Ramadan Nights Lakemba (which attracted 1.57 million people this year), brought attention and focus to our great
City.

We are always looking for better, smarter ways to improve our services. This includes the use of CCTV and artificial
intelligence to detect, graffiti, potholes, missed bins, abandoned shopping trolleys, and dumped rubbish. Use of
closed circuit cameras resulted in 61% reduction in illegal dumping in City hotspots, and facilitated a deep level
inspection of over 40 kilometres of the City’s drainage network.

                                                                            CITY OF CANTERBURY BANKSTOWN ANNUAL REPORT 2023/24

Awards and Recognition

Council was recognised for its work across a diverse range of activities, including:
•                                                                      Councillor Linda Downey won   the 202       4 Ministers’ Awards for Women in Local Government in the Elected
      Representative  Metro category.
•                                                                        2024 Ramadan Nights Lakemba  had record-breaking attendances of 1.57 million people, surpassing 2023 by
      nearly 200,000 people. The event  won The RH Dougherty Events and Communications Award for ‘Innovation
      in special events’, at the Local Government Week NSW 2023 Awards.
•                                                                        The Flux+Flow exhibition was visited by the Art Gallery of NSW Public Program Team and       based on the visit,
      the feature artist, Kristina Mah, was invited to present three performance art sessions at the Art Gallery of
      NSW.
•                                                                        Project architects for the Hurlstone Memorial Reserve Community Centre won the Small Project Architecture
      Award in the 2024 NSW Architecture Awards for the building’s design. The judges commented that the Centre
      ‘is a joyous and unexpected discovery at the end of a suburban street’ and that the project demonstrates
      ‘what can be achieved by imaginative architects, and a brave client determined to create a project of public
      and community value.’
•                                                                        Punchbowl Children's Centre received an ‘Exceeding National Quality Standards’ rating under the National
      Quality Framework.
•                                                                        With a median determination time of 59 days, CBCity will retain its position as one of the most efficient Group
      Three councils in terms of development application processing.

                                                                              CITY OF CANTERBURY BANKSTOWN ANNUAL REPORT 2023/24



Our C                                                                                                                                                        ity in 202                       4

Proclaimed on the 12 May 2016, the of            City Canterbury Bankstown has a population of nearly 380,000 people,
making it one of the most populous local government areas (LGAs) in New South Wales. Located between eight
and 23 kilometres south-west of the Sydney CBD, its 41 suburbs cover just over 100 square kilometres.

The Darug (Darag, Dharug, Daruk, Dharuk) People were the original inhabitants of the Bankstown and Canterbury
areas for many thousands of years before European settlement. The Darug is the largest Aboriginal language group
in the Local Government Area.

The cultural diversity of the City’s current population is extraordinary with almost 45% of residents born overseas
and 59% speaking a language other than English at home. The City has a vibrant and cosmopolitan feel,                                                                          regularly
celebrates its diversity.

Strategically positioned within Sydney’s primary transport and freight corridors, Canterbury       -Bankstown is
accessible by air, rail, and road, and between 15-30 minutes from Sydney’s (Kingsford Smith) Airport and Port
Botany, and 40-50 minutes from the new B  adgerys Creek Airport. On the far western border of the City lies
Bankstown Airport, one of two leading general aviation airports in NSW and a major centre of economic activity,
aviation training, and recreational flights.

Canterbury-Bankstown is a gateway to western and southern Sydney providing an array of economic
opportunities. There are 17 employment land precincts comprising nearly 1,000 hectares across the City which are
connected by major State and regional roads inc   luding the M5 Motorway, Hume Highway, King Georges Road,
Henry Lawson Drive, Canterbury Road, Roberts Road and Stacey Street. Three rail lines traverse the City: the
Australian Rail Track Corporation (ARTC) freight line, the East Hills (T8) and Bankstown (      T2) and (T3) commuter lines
(T3 currently closed for Metro conversion)   .  When the         Sydney Metro conversion is complete, commuters will
benefit from faster, more frequent services, with better accessibility, on the Bankstown line with a metro train at
least every four minutes.

The new ‘vertical city’ campus of the Western Sydney University in the heart of the Bankstown CBD caters for up to
10,000 students and 700 staff, providing facilities for health, education, manufacturing and IT students.

Canterbury-Bankstown features two significant health precincts -      Canterbury Memorial Hospital in Campsie and
the Bankstown-Lidcombe Hospital in Bankstown. The NSW Government has committed $1.3 billion to redevelop
the Bankstown-Lidcombe Hospital on a new site located at the existing TAFE campus in the Bankstown CBD, and in
March 2024, earmarked $350 million to upgrade Canterbury Memorial Hospital.

The City is part of three main catchment areas with waters flowing to the Duck, Cooks and Georges Rivers. The
Georges River National Park, which covers a significant portion of the south-                                    western sides of the City and the Wolli
Creek Regional Park near the   eastern border in Earlwood, are protected areas featuring diverse ecosystems,
including wetlands, bushland and riverside areas. Over 600 parks, many of scenic, natural or sporting significance,
are dotted throughout the City.

We are a productive City: home to over 50,000 businesses and more than 118,000 local jobs. This results in over $16
billion in output and makes Canterbury         -Bankstown one of the largest economies in NSW, contributing over three
percent of Greater Sydney’s employment. The City is well placed to capitalise on the growth of knowledge
intensive, healthcare and education employment sectors.
We are a fast-growing City: expected to reach 500,000 pe ople in the next 10-15 years.
We are a diverse City: 45% of our population were born overseas and 59            % speak any one of around 100 languages
and dialects. This is almost double the diversity of Greater Sydney.
We are a young City: This presents many opportunities as young people are tech- savvy, innovative and excited
about a future which inspires them to lead.
We are a beautiful City: There are large expanses of native bushland, quality arts and sporting facilities, numerous
recreational parklands and reserves, and access to the Cooks and Georges Rivers.

Your Councillors
Councillors represent the interests of residents and ratepayers, provide leadership and guidance to the
community, and encourage communication between Council and the community.

They make sure that the organisation is heading in the direction that is best for the City making important policy
decisions which determine what services Council will undertake and how the budget is allocated.

During the 2023/24 financial year, Councillor Bilal El-Hayek held the office of Mayor.

The office of Deputy Mayor was held by Councillor Clare Raffan from 1 July 2023 to 11 September 2023,  and
Councillor Rachelle Harika from 11 September 2023 to 30 June 2024.

Integrated P                       lanning and R                       eporting


Communities do not exist in isolation –          they are part of a larger natural, social, economic and political
environment. Council’s plans and strategies also do not exist in isolation –         land use and infrastructure planning
support social, environmental and ec  onomic outcomes, and vice-versa – they are all connected and must
therefore be integrated.
Under the Local Government Act 1993         , councils are required to develop a hierarchy of plans known as the
Integrated Planning and Reporting (IP&R) Framework. IP&R requires councils to draw their various plans together
and understand how they interact.

IP&R also acknowledges that the City is constantly changing and that decisions made now may have a long ‘lead’
time before they are realised in the future. Planning must prepare for a sustainable future, one that ensures that
future generations aren’t left  with an unsustainable legacy. IP&R allows councils to get th e maximum leverage
from their efforts by planning holistically for the future.

Importantly, IP&R opens the way for councils and their communities to have important conversations about
funding priorities, service levels, preserving local identity and planning in partnership for a more sustainable
future. The essentials of the IP&R are                                 shown in the adjacent image. This Annual Report forms part of the perpetual
reporting and review phase shown below.

Council’s IP&R obligations are detailed in Section 8c of the Local Government Act 1993         , which outlines the
principles for strategic planning that must be applied to the IP&R Framework. These principles are to:
•                                                                               Iden tify and prioritise  key local community nee ds and aspir ations an d con sider  regional pr iorities;
•                                                                               Iden tify str ategic goals to mee t th ose  needs and aspir ation s;
•                                                                  Deve lop activities, and prioritise actions, to work  towards the strategic goals;
•                                                                         Ensure that the strategic goals and activities to work towards them may be achieved within Council resources;
•                                                                               Regular ly revie w and e valuate  progress towards achie ving str ategic goals;
•                                                                               Maintain an integrated approach to planning, delivering, monitoring and reporting on strategic goals;
•                                                                               Collabor ate  with  others to maximise
         achie vemen t of  s trategi c goals ;
•                                                                               Manage risks to the local community or
         area or to the Coun cil effe ctive ly and
         proactively; an d
•                                                                               Make appr opriate  eviden ce-based
         adaptations to meet changing needs
         and cir cumstances.

Decisions made by Council should:
•                                                                   Recognise diverse local community
         needs and interests;
•                                                                         Consider social justice prin ciples –
         access, e quity, righ ts and participation;
•                                                                         Consider the long term and cumulative
         effects of actions on future
         generations;
•                                                                         Consider the principles of ecologically
         sustain able de ve lopment; and
•                                                                              Be transparent and accountable in
         decision-making.

Integrated P                       lanning and R                       eporting

The Community Strategic Plan (CBCity 2036)
CBCity 2036 guides Canterbury-Bankstown for the next
decade and beyond on its journey to be a thriving,
dynamic and real city of people who are interested and
interesting – unapologetically themselves.

It is based on thousands of conversations with residents,
businesses and government agencies, and interprets
their vision into a blueprint to transform Canterbury     -
Bankstown.

CBCity 2036 is for the people who live, visit and work in Canterbury–Bankstown now and in the future. These
people want what everybody wants  to be happy, healthy and safe in a community that:

•                                                                               Provide s f or their  needs;
•                                                                               Value s their  culture, religion , an d heritage ;
•                                                                               Respects the environment;
•                                                                               Considers the future; and
•                                                                               Respects  the  p as t.

Council’s response to CBCity 2036 can be found in
CBCity 2025 –         the combined Delivery Program and
Operational Pl                                                                                   an, updated and adopted each June.

The Delivery Program
The Delivery Program examines the important issues
facing the Council and outlines the priorities for the
Council term to ensure that services continue to meet
community expectations in terms of quality and value
for money.
The Operational Plan
Annual Operational Plans expand on the priorities in the
Delivery Program by identifying the specific services and
projects Council will provide annually.

The Resourcing Strategy
Other supporting strategies and plans ensure that
Council’s work is integrated and well planned, chief
amongst these, being the Resourcing Strategy, which
comprises a 10-year Asset Management Plan, 10-year
Long Term Financial Plan and a three-year Workforce
Strategy. The Resourcing Strategy ensures that Council
has all of the resources it needs to deliver on its
commitment to the community.

plus a range of internal services  . These services need to be effective and efficiently provided and their progress
and achievements monitored and reported to our community.

Statutory and Corporate   Information
Act ss 428(3), 428 (4)(b) a nd Essential Element 5.2, 5.3 –         Integrated Planning and Guidelines

Service Reviews
The Integrated Planning and Reporting (IP&R) Guidelines (2021) include a requirement for all councils to
undertake service reviews. As part of this review process, it is                                        recommended that the findings of these reviews
are reported to the Audit, Risk and Improvement Committee (ARIC).

Council is committed to evolving our services so that we can continue to respond to the needs of the community.
Our community is diverse and changing rapidly –          as a result, expectations around what th e services Council
provides and how, when and where we p   rovide them also changes. To do this, we are constantly checking in and
reviewing what we do, by:

•                                                           Understanding how, when and where we provide each service, and who else might provide the service        ;
•                                                           Mapping out key processes associated with each service;
•                                                           Understanding the performance of the service (e.g. through surveys, looking at participation trends and
        other measures);
•                                                           Understanding the service’s customers, including who and where they are;
•                                                           Understanding the costs associated with providing our services; and
•                                                           Looking for innovative or different ways to provide a service, and whether the service still has a role in the
        modern day council.

Sometimes we might just look at one aspect of a service, and sometimes we can undertake a more
comprehensive service review, while involves looking how all these elements listed above fit together. A service
review will then make recommendations about future service provision.

In line with this, the results of services reviews in 2023/24 included:

•                                                                   Completion of the Verge Mowing Service Review, with presentation to the ARIC in October 2023;
•                                                                   Preparation of the final Meals on Wheels service report for internal review (will be presented to ARIC in
        2025); and
•                                                                   Continued development of a matrix to prioritise future service reviews.

In 2024/25, Council will particularly focus on the following areas:
1.                                                     Developing a four-year service review program for 2025  -2029;
2.                                          Reviewing the current servicing and maintenance of playgrounds and play spaces across the City;
3.                                            Completing the Meals on Wheels Service Review; and
4.                                         Implementing priority recommendations from the Waste and Cleansing Operations Continuous Improvement
          Plan.

Advisory Committees

Community Advisory Committees or working groups are established by Council to facilitate participation by
members of the community in the development and effective delivery of Council services, policies and
programs.

Community advisory committees work within agreed terms of reference to:
•                                                           Facilitate innovation, new ide as and approaches;
•                                                           Share information amongst key stakeholders;
•                                                           Be representative of and conduct advocacy on behalf of the community to Council;
•                                                           Provide opportunities for stakeholders, including residents and partner organisations, to participate in
        decisions of Council by providing advice and making recommendations; and
•                                                           Contribute to the capacity of the organisation by evaluating the effective delivery of services, policies and
        programs.

Decisions of community advisory committees and working groups are recommendations which may or may not
be adopted or amended by Council. Current Advisory Committees and Working Groups are:

•                                                           Arts and Culture;                                      •                                                           First Peoples;
•                                                           City Marketing and Investment;                         •                                                          Lakemba Ramadan Event;
•                                                           Community and Inclusion;                               •                                                           Traffic (Statutory Committee);
•                                                           Community Safety;                                      •                                                           Universal Access; and
•                                                          Environment;                                            •                                                          Youth.


Audit, Risk and Improvement Committee
The Audit, Risk and Improvement Committee is an independent advisory committee, formed in accordance with
the Local Government Act 1993 and the Local Government (General) Regulation 2021            , to continuously review and
provide independent advice to Council on how it is functioning and managing risk.

The Committee consists of three independent external members, and in March 2022 was appointed for a three         -
year term, which                                                                     ends in March 2025. The Committee meets on a quarterly basis with remuneration at $2,000 per
meeting for independent members and $2,500 for the chairperson. Its Charter is reviewed upon appointment.

Southern Sydney Regional Organisation of Councils (SSROC)
SSROC provides a forum for the exchange of ideas between member councils and an interface between
governments, other councils and key bodies on issues of common interest. It acts as a facilitator for joint activities
between councils through joint contracts which provides benefits through economies of scale. Member councils
can reduce costs of procurement, share the costs of engaging external assistance, and access a wide network of
expertise and views on local government issues.

SSROC also provides a means of resolving issues and challenges that cross municipal boundaries, such as the
environment and transport. Council’s representatives are the Mayor and one Councillor, as well as their two
alternate delegates.

Community Engagement

Council is committed to ongoing and meaningful engagement with our communities and stakeholders. Engaging
with communities helps Council to:

 •                                                                   Identify and understand what is important to our communities -          their needs, priorities and aspirations;
 •                                                                   Ensure that services best meet the range of community needs -             inclusive of cultural and social backgrounds;
 •                                                                   Allow a range of voices to be heard, not just those people who are articulate, angry, loud or with influence;
 •                                                                   Identify shared values, benefits and outcomes, and how Council and community can work together to realise
           goals;
 •                                                                   Increase the community’s understanding of local government; and
 •                                                                   Manage risks by understanding and anticipating issues before they escalate.

During 2023/24, Council held 205 hours of face to face community engagement, 516 hours of digital engagement,
and the engagement Kombi was out in the streets on 44 occasions.


Have Your Say Portal
Council’s Have Your Say online portal   is a centralised hub for public consultations where interested parties can
find out about current initiatives or issues, be informed about activities in their local area, and share views and
ideas. It is a way for the community to speak and for the Council to listen, ensuring that different points of view are
considered before decisions are made. During 2023/24, 78 projects were exhibited for public comment on the
Have Your Say Portal involving 41,093 downloads of information from the site. Projects includ ed:

SECTION 356 DONATIONS AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
Local Government Act 1993 s 356

Local Government Regulation 2021,                                               s 217(1)(a5)

Council’s Community Grants and Events Sponsorship Policy is the governing framework for the provision of financial
assistance to eligible applicants. Funds are distributed under the provisions of Section 356 of the Local Government
Act 1993.

The Policy ensures Council’s administration of financial assistance is conducted in a consistent, equitable,
transparent and financially sustainable manner to provide maximum public benefit in enhancing community
wellbeing in Canterbury -Bankstown.

The Policy provides for funding assistance in an annual Community Grants and Events Sponsorship Program, an Out
of Round Funding Program, donations to appeals for emergency relief, remembrance services, and promotion of
local charities.

Funds distributed under Section 356 of the Local Government Act 1993 in 2023/24 totalled                           $1,422,000. This includes
$521,368 for 129 projects in the 2023/24 annual Community Grants and Events Sponsorship program. Funding for the
2023/24 annual Community Grants and Events Sponsorship Program was requested at a ratio of $3.37 for every $1
available. Approved funding was distributed across the following categories:




Arts and Cultural                                                                                                       $34,600


General Community                                                                                                      $260,073


Event Sponsorship                                                                                                       $63,768


Sport and Recreation                                                                                                    $50,700


Youth                                                                                                                   $78,130


Fee Waiver/Subsidy                                                                                                      $34,097

DISABILITY INCLUSION ACTION PLAN

Disability Inclusion Act 2014, s 13(1)

In 2021, over 25,000 (6.8%) of the population in the Canterbury     -Bankstown
local government area reported needing help in their day to day lives in
areas such as self-care, physical movement or communications. This is
higher than average of Greater Sydney (   5.4% of the population).

11% or 32,820 people aged 15+ also stated that they provided unpaid care
giving highlighting the crucial role that carers play in our community.

As our population ages, the number of people needing assistance in their
day-to-day lives, and the responsibilities of care givers, is likely to
increase, and this will have implications for Council, service providers
and the general community.

In 2022, Council adopted a new Disability Inclusion Action Plan (DIAP).
The Plan reflects the needs of people with disability living in, working in
and visiting Canterbury-Bankstown and focuses on that everyone in our
community, regardless of disability, can live more freely and equally.

The Disability Inclusion Action Plan 2022-26 sets direction and actions under four pillars:

 1.                                                     We will foster positive attitudes and behaviours;
 2.                                          We will create liveable communities;
 3.                                            We will increase opportunities for employment; and
 4.                                         We will improve our systems and processes.


 During 2023/24, Council:
•                                                           Appointed new Access and Inclusion Officer;
•                                                           Convened Universal Access Advisory Committee meetings;
•                                                           Held four community conversations with People with Disability Australia -          20 community members attended;
•                                                           Worked in partnership with Liverpool and Fairfield Councils to hold the South Western Sydney Disability Forum;
•                                                           Convened Social Planning Workshops with 17 attendees from the disability sector;
•                                                           Held the International Day of People with Disability Event for 80 attendees, and held an event for 65 community
       sector workers called “You CAN Ask That” in partnership with CB Disability Abuse Prevention Collaborative;
•                                                           Finalised and distributed Accessible Events Guidelines and checklists, and a Disability Language Guide,
       including internal training for 415 staff;
•                                                           Supported local businesses through the Zero Barriers program;
•                                                           Ensured that people with disability were included in Council-run events and panel discussions;
•                                                           Ensured Council-run major events provided access for people with disability, and included access features in
       promotional material;
•                                                           Held an Accessibility Training workshop for youth workers -              15 attendees;
•                                                           Held the first annual Accessible Library Open Day at Bankstown Library and Knowledge Centre which featured
       an inclusive storytime, and speakers with lived experience -                                          30 attendees;.
•                                                           Facilitated swimming lessons for children who require additional support through the weekly Rainbow Club
       held at Max Parker Leisure and Aquatic Centre;
•                                                           Provided opportunities for Council Learn to Swim instructors to upskill in courses promoting  accessibility and
       inclusion- ten instructors are currently qualified to instruct these lessons and 33 instructors have accessed the
       training;
•                                                           Partnered with Inclusion Works to conduct user testing with individuals that have intellectual disabilities to seek
       feedback on Council’s recruitment process and to implement strategies to improve recruitment processes
       including accessible job postings, accessible application pr ocesses, better collaboration  with community
       organisations, and improved training for Managers  for insights into creating an inclusive interview/shortlisting
       process;

COMPANION ANIMALS
Local Government Regulation 2021,                                               s 217(1)(f)

Companion Animals Act 1998 - Guidelines

In Canterbury -Bankstown, effective companion animal
management is crucial, as evidenced by the presence of
nearly 44,000* registered or identified dogs and cats,
including 23,700 dogs and 20,200 cats. The most common
cat breeds are Ragdoll, British Shorthair, Burmese and
Persian, and the most popular dog breeds are German
Shepherd, Staffordshire Bull Terriers, Maltese                                 and
Labrador Retrievers.

Council incurred costs of $512,017 for companion animal
management, including the care of animals at our holding
facility, while income from animal registrations was
$178,957.

Promoting Responsible Ownership
Council is dedicated to fostering responsible pet
ownership through a diverse range of initiatives. Council
hosts a "Pets Day Out" event which engages directly with
pet owners and distributes educational materials. Social
media is used to share educational content and reminders
about the legal obligations of pet ownership like
microchipping and lifetime registrations. Council’s
Regulatory Services officers emphasise  the importance of
maintaining accurate microchip records when they are out
in the community, significantly increasing the chances of
reuniting lost animals with their owners.

Regulatory Services and Animal Control
Council is committed to ensuring compliance with companion animal regulations. Personalised reminders for
microchipping and registration obligations is provided and and pet owners are educated on the importance of
accurate microchip records. Through proact   ive patrolling of off-leash parks, Animal Control Officers and Rangers
engage with dog owners to promote responsible pet ownership. They also address issues related to stray and
unregistered animals and respond to residents' concerns regarding disruptive p      ets in the community.


Addressing Public Nuisance Concerns
In response to residents' concerns regarding pet    -related nuisances in public areas, Council is proactively
implementing measures. New signage has been installed  and targeted social media campaigns emphasise owner
responsibilities and expectations. Additionally, educational flyers are distributed in areas where issues have been
identified.

Managing Stray Animals
Council’s approach to stray animals prioritises their welfare and responsible pet ownership. Stray dogs identified by
Animal Control Officers and Rangers undergo microchip checks and are reunited with their owners whenever
possible. If an animal is unregistered or the owner cannot be located, it is transported to the Council Animal Holding
Facilities in Rossmore. To deter owners from allowing unrestrained pets, penalties may be imposed owners whose
dogs are found in public areas without restraint.

*Estimates based on November 2024 access to the Office of Local Government Pet registry Database

•                                            Peter Moore Field –          Tudor Street, Belmore;

•                                            The Vale of Ah –           Auld Avenue, Milperra; and
•                                                Virginius Reserve – Virginius Avenue, Padstow.


Animal Holding Facilities
Council has partnered with Rossmore Veterinary Hospital, which provides animal holding facilities to temporarily
house, release, rehome, or, in exceptional cases, euthanise companion animals from our locality. Unclaimed animals
are rehomed through advertis ing and partnerships with reputable rescue organisations.

Euthanasia Policy
Euthanasia is reserved for animals that are severely injured, terminally ill without hope of recovery, or pose a threat
to public safety. These decisions are made following thorough assessments, involving veterinary consultations, to
ensure ethical and res ponsible outcomes.

Education and Off-Leash Parks
To nurture a culture of responsible pet ownership, Council conducts educational initiatives in local parks and
designated off-leash areas. Pet owners are informed of their leash control responsibilities and provided with
information outlining ownership obligations.

Pop-up microchipping and information days are held throughout the City, as well as a Pets Day Out event in May 2024
which featured guest speakers, advice from the Canterbury SES on managing pets during storms and floods, dog
training tips, pet first-aid advice from the Animal Referral Hospital, the 500 Paws Walk, a best dressed competition,
and free microchipping for local pets.

Community Animal Welfare Scheme (CAWS) Campaign
In collaboration with the RSPCA, the Community Animal Welfare Scheme (CAWS) Campaign offers a subsidised
desexing program for the pets of residents with pension, healthcare, or new start cards. This initiative provides
affordable pet healthcare while reducing the number of abandoned animals. In the past year, the campaign
successfully desexed 425 animals and provided 349 82% of those animals with vital vaccinations. A further 89% of
cats and 20% of dogs that were not microchipped at the time of desexing, were able to be chipped.

INSPECTIONS OF PRIVATE SWIMMING POOLS

Swimming Pools Act 1992 (SP Act), s 22F(2)

Swimming Pools Regulation 2018 (SP Reg) cl 23

Pool safety legislation was developed to enhance the safety and security of children under five years old around
private pools. Safety and security measures, including signage, access and barriers (fencing) for pools are required to
be complied with under the provisions of the Swimming Pools Act 1992 and                              Swimming Pools Regulation 2008.

The owner of a swimming pool has the responsibility to ensure that the pool is at all times surrounded by a complying
child-resistant pool safety barrier. Pool safety barriers must be maintained in a good state of repair as an effective and
safe barrier re stricting access to the pool.

Council is required to be notified of the installation of a pool. This notification is achieved via the pool approval and
certification process. Pools are also required to be recorded in the NSW Swimming Pool Register. Council’s Swimming
Pool and Spa Barrier Inspection Program was developed in consultation with the community and was designed to
prevent drownings. It applies to all pools and spas which hold more than 30 centimetres of water, including those that
are portable and inflatable.

A $150 fee applies for the first inspection and $100 if a second inspection is required. If a pool or spa complies, a
certificate of compliance is issued which is valid for three years.

Council also conducts inspections of swimming pools at tourist, visitor and multi-             occupancy developments.

WORKFORCE STRATEGY AND EQUAL OPPORTUNITY EMPLOYMENT


Local Government Regulation 2021 s 217(1)(a9)

WORKFORCE STRATEGY


Council adopted its current Workforce Strategy (2022–2025) in June 2022. This strategy addresses the essential
people resourcing needs required to deliver Council’s Delivery Program and focuses on three key People Priority
Areas:

1.                                                 Inspiring our people with a       mbition and p                                       urpose - engaging our people to create a great city we love.
2.                                       Reimagining our workplace culture -        empowering our people to make a difference.
3.                                        Improving the way we do things -        boosting employee digital dexterity and supporting a growth mindset.

Each priority area includes strategies and actions designed to meet both the current and future workforce planning
needs of Council. The following summary provides key highlights from the current Workforce Management Strategy
for the annual reporting perio  d.

Objective One: Inspiring our people with a                mbition a nd purpose - engaging our people to create a great
city we love

BECOMING A PURPOSE-                            LED ORGANISATION
A strategic priority for Council is to become a purpose -led organisation, recognising the community at the core of
everything we do. A purpose-led focus delivers clear benefits for the community, including increased community
engagement and trust, higher employee satisfaction, and improved organisational performance through innovation.

In June 2024, Council unveiled its new purpose and
ambition, and introduced it across all levels of the
organisation. It marked the beginning of a purpose -led
journey, with plans for deeper integration over the
coming years. The aim is to embed the purpose  and
ambition into employee culture and daily working
practices.

The Purpose is the ‘why’, the driving force behind
action, while our Ambition serves as a promise to the
community, guiding the vision for the future.

EMPOWERING LEADERSHIP TO SERVE OUR COMMUNITY

Leadership At All Levels
Council’s Leadership at All Levels philosophy continues to set clear expectations for our people at all levels across
the organisation, promoting self                                     -leadership, accountability, and personal responsibility. This leadership mindset
applies to both individual wor k and collaborative work across all teams. Aligned with this philosophy is capability
framework, which guides workforce by promoting essential skills and behaviours required for success.

In 2023/24, Council introduced several initiatives to strengthen leadership across the organisation:
•                                                                   New leadership programs providing enhanced resources and learning opportunities;
•                                                                   A revamped Leadership Fundamentals session, with 22 new leaders participating in an updated version that
       included “Leadership Learning Bites” –         concise, focused lessons on key leadership skills;
•                                                                   Personalised coaching for selected leaders, helping them to navigate challenges and grow in their roles; and
•                                                                   Managing Emotional Situations workshops for Open Spaces and Building leaders, attended by 77 leaders and
       high-performing team members. These workshops, now available to all leaders, equipped participants with tools
       to manage emotionally challenging situations with confidence and empath y.

Leadership Forums
In 2023/24, Council held two Leadership Development Forums to strengthen collaboration and focus on strategic
alignment among our 220+ leaders. These forums focused on integrating the Purpose and Ambition, while reinforcing
the importance of placing the customer and community at the heart of what Council does.

1.                                                      Exploring Purpose at CBCity | October 2023 - this forum launched the new Purpose and Ambition, helping
       leaders understand how to embed these principles within their teams.
2.                                          Leading with Purpose | April 2024 -        focused on guiding leaders through transitioning teams to a purpose -driven
       culture and aligning individual actions with the Purpose.

The forums enabled leaders to explore how their actions drive community outcomes and foster a purpose-led culture.

Aspiring Leaders Program
CBCity’s Aspiring Leaders Program continued to empower high -performing employees by developing leadership
capabilities that benefit both the Council and the broader community. Participants engage in  a corporate project,
attend learning sessions with executives, and graduate with a Diploma in Leadership and Management. In 2023/24,
key enhancements to the program included:
•                                                                 Personalised one-on-one external coaching;
•                                                                   DISC assessments                          for better self-                     awareness and communication skills;
•                                                                   Professional development in areas such as emotional intelligence, project management and presentation skills;
       and
•                                                                   Opportunities for public speaking through panel participation, and involvement in Leadership Forums.

During the year, 13 participants were enrolled in the program. Four progressed into full       -time leadership roles, and 50%
of the cohort gained valuable experience acting in leadership positions.

DIVERSITY AND INCLUSION
Council is dedicated         to fostering a culture of Diversity and Inclusion within our workforce. This commitment extends
to ensuring Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) and strives to provide a work environment that fosters fairness,
equity and safety for our diverse workforce.

Disability and Inclusion Action Plan (DIAP)
The Disability and Inclusion Action Plan (DIAP) 2022-2026 supports the objectives and initiatives identified in the EEO
Management Plan.

This year, Council developed a Disability Language Guide        plus an Accessible Events Guide        as a part of the 2022-2026
DIAP. These guides enhanced employees’ understanding and awareness of disability issues while encouraging
thoughtful considerations, terminology and event planning.               Other activities included:
•                                                                   Disability and Inclusion Awareness Training for new staff;
•                                                                   Compulsory Targeted Training for customer-facing staff and event coordinators. Around 400 staff have
        completed this training;
•                                                                   Gender Bias and Inclusive Workplaces Training (33 employees attending the workshop);
•                                                                 Ongoing communication across internal channels, including dedicated intranet pages; and
•                                                                   Ensuring all events held at Council adhere to the “Accessible Events Guidelines and Checklists”.

Ongoing Diversity Initiatives
In addition to the DIAP, Council promotes diversity through various activities including:
•                                                                   Promotion of diversity                                         initiatives through regular communication across internal channels   ; and
•                                                                 Internal training/professional development workshops, such as diversity in the w                                                                                                      orkplace were offered as part of
        an ongoing staff training calendar and were open to all staff.

Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO)
Council is committed to maintaining a working environment free from discrimination, and where team members are
treated fairly, with dignity and respect. This achieved through several initiatives and actions including:
•                                                                   Ensuring all team members have equal access to workplace employment and development opportunities which
        support morale and motivation through increased confidence in leadership and work practices;
•                                                                   Reviewing employment practices regularly to ensure flexibility in accommodating the changing needs of team
        members;
•                                                                   Staying up to date with legislative requirements and ensuring consistency is applied across policies, procedures
        and practices;
•                                                                   Applying merit-based principles to employment decisions to ensure all team members have equal opportunity;
        and
•                                                                   Providing a safe and productive working environment for all team members.

Objective Two: Reimagining workplace culture -                                                                      empowering people to make a difference

To thrive, Council is building an environment where all team members are connected to shared values, and feel
empowered to contribute meaningfully. Council fosters a purpose -driven, customer-focused culture where

CULTURE
Regular engagement using the Net Promoter Score (NPS) is used at key staff events. In November 2023, the ‘CEO
That’s a Wrap’ event achieved an NPS* of 53, reflecting strong engagement across the organisation, underscoring the
importance of celebrating achievements and fostering a positive organisational culture.

Overall, this score forms a strong foundation for continued efforts to build an empowered, purpose       -driven culture,
actively engaging employees in our Purpose to create ‘a great city we love’           .

What is NPS? The Net Promoter Score (NPS)  measures the likelihood of participants recommending an employer.
Scores range from -          100 to +100, with positive scores indicating good engagement and 50+ indicating excellent
engagement.

RECONCILIATION ACTION PLAN (RAP)
In partnership with Reconciliation Australia, Council  is committed to reconciliation and fostering opportunities for
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Innovate         Reconciliation Action Plan (RAP) 2024-26, a public
commitment to reconciliation and an acknowledgment of the rich cultures, histories, and contributions of First
Nations peoples, commenced development in 2023/24.

The RAP Working Group, consisting of representatives from across the organisation and including senior leaders and
frontline workers, worked together to develop the draft plan. Members also completed cultural awareness training.

Other progress in reconciliation efforts, included National Reconciliation Week initiatives, which embraced cultural
acknowledgements as part of important meetings and staff events, and engagement with Dharug Elders in the naming
of key workspaces in the B ankstown Civic Tower in the Dharug language:
•                                                             Iyora/Kitchen – Iyora, Dharug for “people”;
•                                                              Gumal/Meeting Room –                                                     Gumal, Dharug for “friendship”;
•                                                              Yarramundi/Large Collaboration Space –        Yarramundi, Dharug for “storyteller”;
•                                                              Muru/Small Collaboration Space –        Muru, Dharug for “path”; and
•                                                              Bunyuwal/Training Room –                                                     Bunyuwal, Dharug for “learn/teach”.

A National Reconciliation Event, attended by 50 team members, included an interactive rock painting session by a
local Indigenous artist. Over 80% of surveyed attendees reported an improved understanding of reconciliation
following the event.

people is important to us. In the past year, Council had the privilege of celebrating 68 t                                                               eam members for their long
service to our community, spanning milestones of 10, 20, 30 and 40 years of service. This reflects our appreciation for
the contributions of our team members who play a pivotal role in supporting the community.

TRAINEE, APPRENTICE AND GRADUATE PROGRAM (TAG)
The Trainee, Apprentice, and Graduate (TAG) Program continued to provide valuable work opportunities for students
and early career professionals across a range of disciplines. The program offered on-the-job training, mentoring, and
formal qualifications, helping participants develop practical skills and kickstart their careers within local government.

In 2023/24, Council onboarded 11 new entrants across diverse roles and professions, with one graduate already
transitioned into a full-time permanent role before completing their graduate program.

By providing structured training, mentoring, and professional development, the TAG Program strengthens Council’s
talent pipeline, enhances workforce diversity, and ensures we continue to meet the evolving needs of the community.

WORK EXPERIENCE
To connect academic learning with professional experience, Council fosters strategic partnerships with schools and
universities. As part of these educational support initiatives, Council conducts an annual Work Experience P          rogram
every July. In 2023/24,  20 students gained valuable opportunities through this program.

Both the Work Experience Program and the TAG Program enhance students' professional journeys and encourage
collaboration between academia and local government.

HEALTH AND WELLBEING
The strategic direction ‘Wellbeing at CBCity’, developed in 2021, continued to focus on physical, social (inclusion and
connectedness), mental health management, and better integration and connection of staff wellbeing into our
current business practices.

In 2023/24, the following initiatives were implemented:
•                                                                   An annual wellbeing program and calendar;
•                                                                   Execution of year three of the Health and Wellbeing strategy 2021    -2025;
•                                                                   An enhanced intranet mental health platform (Mental Health @CBCity) with information and resources to
       effectively manage mental health, or support for someone seeking help;
•                                                                   Design and implementation of a Social and Emotional Wellbeing Framework;
•                                                                   Delivery of Psychosocial Risk Management Training for leaders;
•                                                                   Delivery of Mental Health First Aid Training (including refresher training);
•                                                                   Partnering with business units across the organisation such as Leisure and Aquatics to allow for optimum use of
       available resources;
•                                                                   High Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) and Yoga sessions offered through the Refresh Program;
•                                                                   Blended (onsite and virtual) initiatives and offerings; and
•                                                                   Program evaluation through the annual Refresh Health and Wellbeing survey.

During 2023/24, Council implemented controls to ensure compliance to new legislative requirements in the
management of psychosocial risk . This included an organisational Social and  Emotional Wellbeing survey,
organisational risk profiling, risk action planning, and the design and development of a Social and Emotional Wellbeing
Framework to ensure ongoing knowledge, support and guidance in relation to the psychosocial health.

WORKPLACE RELATIONS
Council’s Consultative Committee (CC) is an internal representative body that meets regularly to discuss and resolve
organisational-                                          wide issues. The committee is integral to workforce relations, provides an important voice for team
members, and assists Council to mitigate issues.

The Committee plays a key role in the review of human resource related policies and procedures, seeking feedback

policies and procedures, and discussed 23 agenda items.

EMPLOYEE ASSISTANCE PROGRAM (EAP)
Prioritising the mental and emotional wellbeing of team members remains at the forefront of the Council's agenda.
Council is committed to fostering a supportive environment, and consistently offer a confidential counselling and
referral service, benefittin g not only team members but also their immediate families. The Employee Assistance
Program (EAP) stands as a vital pillar, underpinning a wide spectrum of operations, from everyday personnel
interactions to more comprehensive change management initiatives.

The EAP’s multifaceted support, ranging from crisis management and developmental coaching,                                              to career guidance,
conflict resolution, managerial assistance, and carer support, underscores its importance in enhancing our staff's
overall wellbeing.

female colleagues at Council. The event focused on the theme, "Count her in: Invest in Women. Accelerate Progress"
and featured a panel of women fr  om the Sydney Women’s Fund Advisory Council. Attended by over 85 people, plus
over 35 watching via livestream, the event was well-received, with attendees finding the panel engaging and inspiring.


Objective Three  -                                                                                       improve the way we do things

DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION
In a rapidly evolving technological landscape, Council is keenly aware of the imperative to remain not only current, but
also forward-thinking. Council is deeply invested in digital transformation, an effort representative of the
commitment to ensuring neither community nor workforce is left in the wake of techno       logy. This transformation is not
just about harnessing the latest technology; it's about redefining responsiveness, agility, and the ease with which
community and partners can engage with Council.

Last year CBCity commenced work on a comprehensive Digital Strategic Plan, integrating multiple forward -looking
strategies like Business Improvement, Information Services, Activating Data Roadmap, and Smart Cities. This unified
approach ensures that Counci  l remains at the cusp of contemporary practices, meeting the digital demands of today,
while pre-empting those of tomorrow.

The groundwork for this transformative shift is rooted in internal and external research, inclusive community
consultations, and thoughtful review of resources. Council recognises that real digital transformation is not just about
technology; it's about people. As such, Council is committed to ensuring teams are set up for success with the
environment and skills needed in this digital age, making Council more efficient, and an easier organisation with which
to do business.

MODERNISING HR SYSTEMS
The shift towards modernising human resource (HR) systems is crucial for effectively managing and engaging with our
most valuable asset—our people. It also plays a key role in attracting new talent to the organisation. Over the past 18
months, Council focused on streamlining processes and modernizing HR systems, implementing more efficient
practices, and leveraging technology to enhance the experience for both candidates and emp       loyees.

An all-                                                                 in-one system -        ‘myhr’ -provides real-time workforce data, access to online training, and allows employees to
update personal information, such as bank details, directly, eliminating delays. Additionally, it has improved
recruitment, onboarding, and  offboarding functions, resulting in a smoother candidate experience.

In 2023/24, Council expanded the ‘myhr’ suite by launching three new modules -          Learning, Performance, and
Compensation. This consolidation replaced previous systems, creating a more streamlined and user-friendly process.
For example, the transition of CBCi  ty’s Performance Review process to ‘myhr’ led to a significant increase in
participation, with an 87% completion rate in the first month, compared to just 44% the previous year. This underscores
the positive impact of ‘myhr’ and its accessibility for all users.

CBCity’s ‘myhr’ journey is ongoing, as Council continues to seek opportunities for improvement. In the next phase, the
Time and Attendance module will be implemented which will enhance accessibility for all employees, particularly the
outdoor workforce, who will shift from manual to online timesheets.

EMBEDDING A LEARNING MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (LMS)
The introduction of ‘myhr’ included MyLearning, Council’s first Learning Management System (LMS), designed to
streamline the management of learning assignments, records, and training data. Key achievements so far have
included:
•                                                              Rolling out nine mandatory compliance modules with over 90% completion rates across the organization;
•                                                              Tracking compliance and external professional development training;
•                                                              Recording essential compliance requirements such as First Aid, CPR, and Warden Training;
•                                                              Expanding continuous learning opportunities through workshops and eLearning modules; and
•                                                              Integrating Safety Hub training videos into MyLearning, with 505 modules completed, boosting workplace safety
       awareness.

Phase two is underway, and focusses on finalising training requirements and integrating historical data for role         -
specific learning.

CULTIVATING A GROWTH MINDSET
Council fosters a culture of continuous learning by offering professional development, educational assistance,
mentoring, and leadership training to cultivate a growth mindset among staff. Key achievements last year included:
•                                                              Delivery of  several new face-                               to-face and virtual workshops including Emotional Intelligence (43 attendees),
       Effective Communication (98 attendees), Building Positive Team Dynamics (86 attendees), Dealing with Difficult
       Customers (70 attendees), and Virtual Time Management (19 attendees), with 563 participants attending in -house
       developed workshops across the organisation;
•                                                              Expanding eLearning modules to include Dealing with Customers (49 completions) and Developing a Growth
       Mindset (31 completions), resulting in 787 participants completing eLearning modules;
•                                                              Supporting team members through the Educational Assistance program;
•                                                              Offering external, formal training opportunities, including 10 staff members completing a Certificate IV in
       Leadership and Management; and
•                                                              Developing an Outdoor Future Leaders program for the Open Space and Buildings teams, providing leadership
       and digital literacy skills, with two participants successfully stepping into leadership roles.

SENIOR STAFF REMUNERATION

Local Government Regulation  s 217  (1) (b) (i), (ii), (iii), (iv), (v) and (c) (i), (ii), (iii), (iv), (v)

Employees designated to be senior staff under the Local Government Act 1993 were expected to attend all Council
meetings and be on call. Remuneration is in packaged form and comprises cash, car, fringe benefits tax and

      GOVERNMENT INFORMATION (PUBLIC ACCESS) ACT 2009

      Government Information (Public Access) Act 2009, s 125(1)

      Government Information (Public Access) Regulation 2018, cl 8,  Schedule 2


      In accordance with Section 125 of the Government Information (Public Access) Act 2009 (GIPAA), councils are required
      to report on government information public access activity. Council undertakes a review at least every 12 months to
      identify the kinds of information that can be made publicly available. During the reporting period, this has included:

•                                                                  Ensuring the information published on Council's website is up to date, informative and relevant;
•                                                                   Collecting data on the type/s of information requested to determine how Council can make this an easier process
                             for applicants;
•                                                                  Monitoring matters of public interest to review whether Council can proactively release information; and
•                                                                  Prioritising the development of video content to better inform our community.

In accordance with certain statutory requirements as outlined in the Local Government Act 1993 and Council policies,
Council is required to make necessary adjustments to the level of income received by Council throughout the financial
year, specifically relating to rates and annual charges.

The major component of the adjustments is to reflect the rates and charges written off which are attributable to
pensioners and to those properties that become eligible for exemption from all rates throughout the year in
accordance with the Local Government Act 1993      .

WORKS ON PRIVATE PROPERTY

Local Government Act 1993  s 67, 67(2)(b),67(3)

Local Government (General) Regulation 2021 Reg s 217(1)(a4)
In accordance with Section 67 of the Local Government Act 1993 a council may, by agreement with the owner or
occupier of any private land, carry out on the land any kind of work that may lawfully be carried out on the land.
Examples of the kind of work under this section include:

  •                                                                   Paving and roadmaking;
  •                                                                   Kerb and guttering;
  •                                                                   Fencing and ditching;
  •                                                                   Tree planting and tree maintenance;
  •                                                                   Demolition and excavation;
  •                                                                   Land clearing and tree felling;
  •                                                                   Water, sewerage and drainage connections; and
  •                                                                   Gas and electricity connections.

This work is carried out in accordance with Council’s adopted Fees and Charges and does not apply to work carried
out by a council, or by two or more councils jointly, for another council or for a public authority, or for any graffiti
removal work carried out in accordance with Part 4 of the Graffiti Control Act 2008               .

Any works to be carried out on private property that would not be in accordance with Council’s adopted Fees and
Charges would require a resolution of Council. In this regard, Council made no resolutions in 2023/24.

ASSET MANAGEMENT
Council the custodian of an extensive range of assets that assist in delivering services to the community. These assets,
which play an integral part in the lives of residents and visitors alike, are used daily and are under constant pressure to
be operational, accessible and compliant. Council’s extensive $         5 billion (gross replacement cost) asset portfolio
includes:
•                                                                   Infrastructure like roads, footpaths, drains and parks;
•                                                                   Community buildings like parks amenities, town halls and community centres;
•                                                                   Operational buildings and plant and equipment;
•                                                                   Natural and heritage assets; and
•                                                                   Some residential and commercial properties.

Council is strongly committed to delivering high quality assets and services to the community and complying with its
legislative requirements. As part of its Resourcing Strategy, Council adopted a revised 10 -year Asset Management
Strategy in June 2024 to guide and shape the short, medium and long-term planning of assets, and ensure sustainable
service delivery for both current and future generations in the City. The Strategy works towards:
 •                                                              Better outcomes: improving services through better alignment of customer needs and future asset provision;
 •                                                              Informed decision making: using data to make better decisions regarding asset use, condition and management;
 •                                                              Sustainable lifecycle management: ensuring assets are managed in a manner that is socially, financially and
          environmentally sustainable throughout their life;
 •                                                              Improved budget allocation: assigning appropriate funding for the renewal, upgrade and maintenance of
          existing assets;
 •                                                              Prioritised maintenance: using a proactive approach to maintain assets in line with identified service levels;
 •                                                              Understanding limitations: clearly defining service levels and determining what can be delivered with the
          available financial and physical resources; and
 •                                                              Minimising risk: identifying and planning for potential asset related risks.

2023/24 Capital Program
Each year, Council allocates funds as part of its Operational Plan to provide new or upgraded infrastructure for our
community, including playgrounds, sport and recreation facilities, community buildings, roads, footpaths and
pedestrian facilities.  This program of works continues to enhance our City now and into the future, ensuring
Canterbury-Bankstown remains a great place to live, work and play.
During 2023/24, Council invested over $70.9 million in projects across Canterbury -Bankstown including:
•                                                                  $13.6 million f or  c        ommunity and park                                          buildings, including l                                                                     eisure and aquatic                                    facilities
•                                                                  $15.5 million for p                                       arks, playgrounds and sporting                                                                  facilities
•                                                                  $19.3 million f or  r        oad, footpath, carpark, bridge and t                                                                        raffic upgrades
•                                                                  $7.4 million for s         tormwater Improvements

Expenditure Guidelines issued by the Office of Local Government under Section 23A of the Local Government Act 1993
in December 2010. The Canterbury Leisure and Aquatic Centre      project meets                          the criteria for the that           reporting in

Asset Condition
A key issue facing local governments throughout Australia is the management of ageing assets i.e. those in need of
renewal and replacement. The overall average condition of Council’s assets portfolio is slowly deteriorating so that
the condition of some assets is now below acceptable standards and some have deteriorated to the point where they
should be (or should have already been) replaced.

The table below, prepared in accordance with Section 428 2(d) of the Local Government Act 1993 as part of Council’s
Financial Statements, details asset condition, the current replacement cost for each of Council’s asset categories,
the calculated funding required for maintenance of each asset category at a satisfactory level, and the estimated
depreciated replacement cost of infrastructure.

It shows that based on the ratings below, 38.6 % of Council’s assets are rated as condition 1 or 2, or ‘better than
satisfactory’; 52.6% are rated satisfactory, and 8.8% are rated either poor or very poor.






























Source: Special Schedule –                                                     audited 2023/24 Financial Statements.

WORKS FUNDED FROM SPECIAL RATE VARIATION–                                                                       Former Canterbury Local
Government Area

Special Rate Variation Guidelines 2020  7.1

In June 2004, following extensive community consultation, the NSW Minister for Local Government approved a
Special Rate Variation (SRV) of 7.5 per cent increase in that year to the former Canterbury City Council, for a period of
15 years, to be used to upgrade roads, footpaths, stormwater drainage, town centres and associated assets. This SRV
expired in 2019.

In February 2014, with the support of local residents of the former Canterbury City Council, the Independent Pricing
and Regulatory Tribunal of NSW approved a further special rate variation of 7.5 per cent each year for three years
including the stipulated annual rate increase prescribed by the NSW Government    .

Since its introduction, this funding has enabled Council to deliver a wide range of projects that have significantly
enhanced community infrastructure and local amenities. Below is a list of design and construction projects that were
undertaken in the former Canterbury Local Government Area during 2023/24 through                        funds generated from the
Special Rate Variation. Each of these projects has contributed to a variety of CBCity 2036 Destination outcomes. The
total value of the works was $ 8,203,105.

The 2023/24 financial year marks the final year in which funds will be allocated from the former Canterbury Special
Rate Variation (SRV). Where SRV funded projects remain in progress at the end of 2023/24, this funding has been
carried over to 2024/25 to e  nable completion of the project .
